idiom_name: Resilience4j RateLimiter (JVM) around suspend/blocking calls; kotlinx.coroutines Semaphore bounds concurrency, not rate
implementation_notes: Kotlin/JVM inherits the JVM limiter ecosystem, so the realistic realization is Resilience4j's RateLimiter (or Guava's) wrapped around the call - the Java decorators accept Kotlin lambdas through SAM conversion and RequestNotPermitted is the refusal to map to 429. The coroutine standard library ships no rate limiter: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore is a fair counting semaphore that bounds concurrent access, which is a concurrency limit, not a rate limit. A coroutine-native limiter is therefore hand-rolled - a Mutex-guarded token count refilled from a monotonic source with delay() between refills - and is only worth it when the call path must suspend rather than block.
pitfalls: Blocking acquisition inside a coroutine pins the dispatcher thread; prefer fail-fast acquisition or a suspending wrapper around the limiter.
Semaphore is not a rate limiter: permitting 100 concurrent callers says nothing about the 100 requests per second the dependency accepts.
Resilience4j limiter state is per instance and per JVM; a limiter created inside a request scope never limits.
